families.topic: transmission, symptoms, hygiene, exclusion, swimming restrictions and recovery from cryptosporidiosis
evidence_points: Cryptosporidium is a parasite that can infect people and some animals.
Potential sources include contaminated water, swimming pools, food, farm animals and contaminated objects.
The most common illness is diarrhoea, which may be accompanied by vomiting or abdominal symptoms.
People with weakened immune systems can be more seriously affected.
Most otherwise healthy people recover without a specific antiparasitic treatment.
Hydration is important because diarrhoea and vomiting can cause fluid and electrolyte loss.
People should remain away from work or school until at least 48 hours after diarrhoea or vomiting stops.
Swimming should be avoided while ill and for 2 weeks after diarrhoea stops.
Symptoms alone do not identify the source of a cryptosporidiosis infection.
Outbreak assessment requires laboratory confirmation, exposure history, timing and epidemiological links.

families.source: UKHSA national contingency plan for invasive Aedes mosquitoes in England
families.topic: surveillance, risk levels, vector control, roles and outbreak response for invasive Aedes mosquitoes and associated diseases
families.page_title: National contingency plan for invasive Aedes mosquitoes in England
evidence_points: The 2026 plan supersedes the 2020 national contingency plan for invasive mosquitoes.
It covers introductions, established invasive Aedes populations and locally acquired human disease.
The plan focuses on Aedes mosquitoes capable of transmitting dengue, chikungunya and Zika.
It defines risk levels from no detection through widespread establishment and local outbreaks.
Early surveillance and rapid response are intended to prevent establishment.
UKHSA coordinates public-health surveillance, risk assessment and incident response.
Local authorities have roles in surveillance, environmental management and vector control.
Actions become more intensive as mosquito establishment and local transmission risk increase.
A single mosquito detection does not by itself prove an established population or local disease transmission.
Response level requires species confirmation, repeated detection, season, geography, human cases and incident-specific risk assessment.

families.source: UKHSA acute respiratory infection outbreak management guidance for care homes
families.topic: case definitions, testing, surveillance, infection control, antivirals and outbreak management in adult care homes
families.page_title: Influenza-like illness (ILI): managing outbreaks in care homes
evidence_points: The guidance covers acute respiratory infection outbreaks in registered adult care homes.
It includes case and outbreak definitions.
It addresses investigation, surveillance and pathogen testing.
It provides infection prevention and control measures for residents and staff.
It supports risk-based and time-limited interventions.
It includes influenza antiviral treatment and prophylaxis considerations.
It addresses hospital admission and discharge during an outbreak.
It recognises that influenza, COVID-19 and other respiratory viruses can co-circulate.
Two respiratory illnesses in a home are not automatically a confirmed single-pathogen outbreak.
Classification requires epidemiological linkage, onset timing, symptoms, testing and health-protection assessment.

families.source: UKHSA suspected acute viral respiratory infection outbreak guidance for schools
families.topic: preparedness, investigation, testing, communication and response for respiratory outbreaks in schools
families.page_title: Suspected acute viral respiratory infections: managing outbreaks in schools
evidence_points: The guidance is for health protection teams assessing suspected acute viral respiratory outbreaks in schools.
It includes preparedness measures before an outbreak.
It provides a framework for investigation of linked illness in pupils and staff.
It addresses response measures and communication with the school community.
The current guidance uses a shorter window for identifying new outbreaks than earlier versions.
Risk assessment considers symptoms, onset dates, absenteeism and epidemiological linkage.
Testing can help distinguish influenza, COVID-19 and other respiratory viruses.
Antiviral treatment may be considered for eligible children in clinical risk groups under national guidance.
Several illnesses occurring in a school do not automatically prove a common outbreak.
Response requires linkage, timing, setting information, laboratory evidence and proportionate health-protection judgement.

families.source: UKHSA influenza antiviral treatment and prophylaxis guidance
families.topic: treatment, post-exposure prophylaxis, resistance, dosing and special-population use of influenza antivirals
families.page_title: Influenza: treatment and prophylaxis using anti-viral agents
evidence_points: The guidance covers antiviral treatment of suspected or confirmed seasonal influenza.
It includes recommendations for post-exposure prophylaxis.
It addresses use during pregnancy, breastfeeding and the neonatal period.
It includes considerations for renal and hepatic dysfunction.
It describes treatment choices for non-severe and severe influenza.
It addresses poor clinical response and possible antiviral resistance.
It includes dosage and schedule recommendations for neuraminidase inhibitors.
It is intended primarily for healthcare professionals and health protection teams in England.
Antiviral eligibility cannot be determined from a positive test or exposure alone.
Treatment decisions require severity, timing, risk group, renal function, resistance context and clinical judgement.
